Another risk includes the failure of check valves which may allow air or moisture into the system which can lead to internal degradation or unpredictable combustion during subsequent operations. Importantly, many of the higher risk scenarios assume that trains come into service with a full or half tank of hydrogen and that defueling and refueling occur indoors. If defueling and refueling were performed outdoors, those “medium” risk scenarios would decrease to a “low” severity rating. This highlights an important aspect of this risk assessment: just because a certain scenario of the HAZOP was rated as “high” or “low” risk, it does not mean that the risk is not changeable. Lower risk scenarios could become higher risk if the design or other factors could lead to additional hazard. These risks are characterized by slow release rates, such as fugitive emissions from unattended rail cars or fuel cell servicing. Because these leaks are typically gradual, they may be detectable as loss of hydrogen line pressure over time or via ambient gas monitoring. Additionally, environmental factors like ice formation or condensation at low temperatures are recognized for their potential to cause mechanical difficulties with connectors and pressure fluctuations during refueling [28]. The lowest-ranked risks involve process inefficiencies and mechanical sticking, such as uncombusted hydrogen in fuel cell exhaust or manual valves that fail to seat perfectly after servicing. These events are categorized as low risk because there are failsafes such as automatic shutoffs in case a leak is detected to ensure that hydrogen is not released.
